USER REQUEST:
Write a polynomial-time reduction from Clique to SAT. problems.py defines both problems: SOURCE is Clique and TARGET is SAT. The SOURCE and TARGET class docstrings give the exact instance formats, yes-conditions and edge cases.

PROBLEM DEFINITIONS (the SOURCE and TARGET docstrings from problems.py, complete as given here):

SOURCE = Clique
Clique.

Instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
  * Vertices are 0..n-1. Edges are undirected pairs [u, v] with u != v;
    [u, v] and [v, u] are the same edge and may not both appear.
  * k is any integer.

Yes iff the graph has a clique of AT LEAST k vertices: k vertices with an
edge between every two of them.

Edge cases: k <= 0 is always yes. k = 1 is yes whenever n >= 1. k > n is
always no.

TARGET = Sat
SAT (CNF satisfiability).

Instance: {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[literal, ...], ...]}
  * Variables are 1..m. A literal is +v (v is true) or -v (v is false).
  * A clause is a list of any number of literals, including none.
    Literals may repeat, and a clause may contain both v and -v.
  * Literal order inside a clause and clause order do not matter. The
    same clause may appear more than once.
  * Variables need not all appear in a clause.

Yes iff some assignment of true/false to variables 1..m makes every
clause contain at least one true literal.

Edge cases: a formula with no clauses is satisfiable (yes). An empty
clause [] can never be satisfied, so any formula containing one is no.

INPUT FILES: ["problems.py"]
WORKING DIRECTORY: /tmp/reduction-hfgavw_0

It provides SOURCE and TARGET with is_yes(instance), validate(instance) and random_instance(rng, scale); search it (e.g. with grep) only if you need something specific.

    reduce(instance) -> instance

The answer to the returned instance must be yes exactly when the answer to the input instance is yes, and reduce must run in polynomial time. Do not call the brute-force solvers inside reduce.

"""Polynomial-time reduction from Clique to SAT.

Clique instance: {"n": n, "edges": [[u, v], ...], "k": k}
SAT instance:    {"num_vars": m, "clauses": [[literal, ...], ...]}

Construction
------------
For a clique of size k we use boolean variables

    x[i][v]  (1-indexed variable i*n + v + 1)

meaning "vertex v is the i-th chosen vertex of the clique",
for i in 0..k-1 and v in 0..n-1.

Clauses:
  * For every position i: (x[i][0] or ... or x[i][n-1])
    (each position must be filled).
  * For every position i and every pair u < v: (~x[i][u] or ~x[i][v])
    (at most one vertex per position).
  * For every pair of positions i < j and every pair (u, v) such that
    u == v or {u, v} is not an edge: (~x[i][u] or ~x[j][v])
    (chosen vertices are pairwise distinct and adjacent).

A satisfying assignment yields k distinct pairwise-adjacent vertices,
i.e. a clique of size k; a clique of size k yields a satisfying
assignment by putting its vertices in the k positions.

Edge cases are handled directly:
  * k <= 0  -> Clique is yes -> return the empty (satisfiable) formula.
  * k >  n  -> Clique is no  -> return a formula with the empty clause.
"""


def reduce(instance):
    n = instance["n"]
    edges = instance["edges"]
    k = instance["k"]

    # k <= 0 is always yes: an empty CNF is satisfiable.
    if k <= 0:
        return {"num_vars": 0, "clauses": []}

    # A clique can never have more than n vertices.
    if k > n:
        return {"num_vars": 0, "clauses": [[]]}

    # Build the undirected adjacency set.
    adjacent = set()
    for u, v in edges:
        adjacent.add((u, v))
        adjacent.add((v, u))

    def var(i, v):
        return i * n + v + 1

    num_vars = k * n
    clauses = []

    for i in range(k):
        # At least one vertex in position i.
        clauses.append([var(i, v) for v in range(n)])
        # At most one vertex in position i.
        for u in range(n):
            for v in range(u + 1, n):
                clauses.append([-var(i, u), -var(i, v)])

    # Cross-position constraints: the i-th and j-th chosen vertices must be
    # distinct and adjacent.
    for i in range(k):
        for j in range(i + 1, k):
            for u in range(n):
                for v in range(n):
                    if u == v or (u, v) not in adjacent:
                        clauses.append([-var(i, u), -var(j, v)])

    return {"num_vars": num_vars, "clauses": clauses}
